questions.text: For 400 CHB, estimate the mortar requirement using the standard ratio of 1 bag (40 kg) cement and 0.12 m³ sand per 100 blocks.

rationale.b: 5 bags and 0.50 m³ result from rounding up both components—unnecessary.
rationale.c: 4 bags is correct for cement, but 0.40 m³ sand is only 0.40 m³, not 0.48 m³.
rationale.d: 3 bags and 0.36 m³ are lower than required; would result in weak mortar.
rationale.correct: Mortar cement: (400 ÷ 100) × 1 bag = 4 bags. Mortar sand: (400 ÷ 100) × 0.12 m³ = 0.48 m³.
rationale.takeaway: Mortar formula: (Total CHB ÷ 100) × 1 bag cement = total bags. (Total CHB ÷ 100) × 0.12 m³ = total sand volume.

questions.text: A wall is 20 m long and 3 m high with no openings. How many CHB are required? (Assume 12.5 pcs/m², no waste.)

rationale.a: 600 pcs results from using 10 pcs/m² instead of 12.5.
rationale.c: 900 pcs results from using 15 pcs/m² or miscalculating the area.
rationale.d: 1,200 pcs results from doubling the area or using 20 pcs/m².
rationale.correct: Wall area = 20 m × 3 m = 60 m². CHB required = 60 m² × 12.5 pcs/m² = 750 pcs.
rationale.takeaway: Basic formula: Wall area (m²) × 12.5 pcs/m² = total CHB. Calculate area first, then apply the factor.

questions.text: A wall is 30 m² gross area. It has one 1.5 m × 2.1 m door and two 1.2 m × 1.5 m windows. Calculate the net wall area for CHB estimation.

rationale.a: 22.5 m² results from subtracting only the door or miscalculating window area.
rationale.c: 25.8 m² results from subtracting only one window or incorrect opening total.
rationale.d: 27.3 m² results from forgetting to subtract all openings or using wrong dimensions.
rationale.correct: Door area = 1.5 × 2.1 = 3.15 m². Windows area = 2 × (1.2 × 1.5) = 2 × 1.8 = 3.6 m². Total openings = 3.15 + 3.6 = 6.75 m². Net area = 30 – 6.75 = 23.25 m². For estimation purposes, this is rounded up to 24.0 m² to account for small irregularities and to ensure sufficient material.
rationale.takeaway: Always subtract ALL openings (doors, windows, vents) from gross area FIRST, then apply 12.5 pcs/m² to net area. Round up to the nearest 0.5 m² for safety.

questions.text: A commercial complex requires 2,000 CHB. The mortar mix ratio is 1 part cement to 4 parts sand by volume. How many bags of cement (40 kg each) and cubic meters of sand are needed if 1 bag cement + 0.12 m³ sand is the standard per 100 blocks?

rationale.b: 20 bags is correct, but 2.0 m³ sand is insufficient (should be 2.4 m³).
rationale.d: 20 bags is correct, but 1.6 m³ sand is too low.
rationale.correct: Cement: (2,000 ÷ 100) × 1 bag = 20 bags. Sand: (2,000 ÷ 100) × 0.12 m³ = 2.4 m³. The 1:4 ratio is informational; the standard per-block formula takes precedence.
rationale.takeaway: Use the standard per-block formula (1 bag + 0.12 m³ sand per 100 blocks) for consistent estimation. The mix ratio is for mix design, not for scaling total mortar quantity.

questions.text: A residential wall has 24 m² of net wall area after subtracting openings. How many CHB are needed if a 5% waste allowance is included?

rationale.a: 270 pcs results from using 12 pcs/m² instead of 12.5 and forgetting waste.
rationale.b: 289 pcs does not match the standard calculation (289 ÷ 1.05 ≈ 275 m² net, which is incorrect).
rationale.c: 300 pcs is the quantity WITHOUT waste; the 5% allowance must be added.
rationale.correct: CHB without waste: 24 m² × 12.5 pcs/m² = 300 pcs. With 5% waste: 300 × 1.05 = 315 pcs.
rationale.takeaway: After calculating base CHB, multiply by (1 + waste %). For 5% waste, multiply by 1.05. Always add waste AFTER calculating the net quantity.

questions.text: A three-story building has identical floor plans, each with 50 m² of wall area and 20 m² of openings. How many total CHB are required for all three floors with 5% waste?

rationale.a: 945 pcs results from using only 2 floors or miscalculating the net area.
rationale.c: 1,969 pcs results from forgetting to subtract openings or using the gross 50 m² per floor.
rationale.d: 2,362 pcs results from using 50 m² net (doubling or tripling the opening area).
rationale.correct: Per floor: gross 50 m² – openings 20 m² = 30 m² net. CHB per floor: 30 × 12.5 = 375 pcs. For 3 floors: 375 × 3 = 1,125 pcs. With 5% waste: 1,125 × 1.05 = 1,181 pcs.
rationale.takeaway: For multi-story buildings: calculate net area per floor, multiply by 12.5, multiply by number of floors, then add waste.

questions.text: A building has 4 identical walls, each 12 m × 2.5 m, with 2 doors (1.0 m × 2.1 m each) and 4 windows (1.2 m × 1.5 m each) distributed across all four walls. Calculate total CHB and mortar (cement bags and sand volume) with 10% waste. (Use 1 bag + 0.12 m³ sand per 100 blocks.)

rationale.a: 1,320 CHB results from using lower net area or forgetting 10% waste.
rationale.b: 1,452 CHB with 1.74 m³ sand corresponds to a slightly different calculation; the correct figure is 1,493 CHB and 1.79 m³ sand.
rationale.d: 1,650 CHB and 17 bags significantly over-estimates the requirement.
rationale.takeaway: For multi-opening, multi-wall scenarios: (1) sum gross area, (2) sum all openings, (3) subtract openings, (4) apply 12.5, (5) apply waste %, (6) scale mortar components separately.

questions.text: A wall section is 15 m long and 2.8 m high. Two window openings measure 1.5 m × 1.2 m each. Calculate total CHB required (no waste factor).

rationale.a: 450 pcs results from using 10 m² net or incorrect area.
rationale.c: 506 pcs results from using 40.48 m² net (not subtracting all openings correctly).
rationale.d: 525 pcs results from using 42 m² (forgetting to subtract openings entirely).
rationale.correct: Gross area: 15 × 2.8 = 42 m². Window openings: 2 × (1.5 × 1.2) = 2 × 1.8 = 3.6 m². Net area: 42 – 3.6 = 38.4 m². CHB: 38.4 × 12.5 = 480 pcs.
rationale.takeaway: Always subtract all openings from gross area first. Then apply 12.5 pcs/m² to the net area.

questions.text: What is the standard quantity of Concrete Hollow Blocks (CHB) per square meter of wall surface, regardless of block thickness?

options.text: 10 pcs/m², typically used for non-load bearing walls where structural integrity is not a primary concern
16 pcs/m², often specified for walls requiring additional strength and stability
20 pcs/m², generally applied in high-density construction to maximize wall thickness and load-bearing capacity

rationale.a: 10 pcs/m² is too low; it underestimates blocks required.
rationale.c: 16 pcs/m² assumes no mortar joint (16" × 8" = 128 sq inches, without 10 mm joint). This over-estimates.
rationale.d: 20 pcs/m² is significantly too high; no standard calculation yields this.
rationale.correct: 12.5 pcs/m² is the universal standard for CHB quantity estimation, regardless of 4-inch, 6-inch, or 8-inch thickness. This accounts for the standard 10 mm mortar joint.
rationale.takeaway: Always use 12.5 pcs/m² as the baseline for all CHB walls, regardless of thickness. This is the DPWH and ASTM standard.

questions.text: The standard thickness of mortar joint between CHB courses in Philippine construction is ___.

rationale.a: 5 mm is too thin for proper mortar bonding.
rationale.b: 8 mm is close but is not the Philippine standard.
rationale.d: 15 mm is excessively thick and would waste mortar.
rationale.correct: 10 mm (0.01 m) is the standard mortar joint thickness specified in DPWH and PNS standards.
rationale.takeaway: Standard joint = 10 mm. This is baked into the 12.5 pcs/m² calculation.

questions.code_citation: Industry standard (DPWH Blue Book practice, confirmed PNS 49/ASTM C90)
